'''''Opuntia engelmannii''''' is a [[opuntia|prickly pear]] common across the south-central and [[Southwestern United States]] and northern [[Mexico]]. It goes by a variety of common names, including '''desert prickly pear''', '''discus prickly pear''', '''Engelmann's prickly pear'''<ref name="grin">{{GRIN | access-date=2013-03-23}}</ref> in the US, and '''nopal''', '''abrojo''', '''joconostle''', and '''vela de coyote''' in Mexico.

The nomenclatural history of this species is somewhat complicated due to the varieties, as well as its habit of hybridizing with ''[[Opuntia phaeacantha]]''. It differs from ''[[Opuntia phaeacantha|O. phaeacantha]]'' by being green year round instead of turning reddish purple during winter or dry seasons, as well as having yellow flowers with red centers.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Felger|first1=R.S|last2=Hawkins|first2=J.A.|last3=Verrier|first3=J.|date=2017-07-18|title=New combinations for Sonoran Desert plants|url=http://www.phytoneuron.net/2017Phytoneuron/48PhytoN-SonoranNames.pdf|journal=Phytoneuron|issue=48|pages=1–6}}</ref>

==Distribution==
''O. engelmannii'' is native to sub-tropical regions of North America. It prefers hot, dry conditions, but is more frost-tolerant than other species of ''Opuntia''.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Pasiecznik |first=Nick |date=2015-01-28 |title=Opuntia engelmannii (cactus apple) |url=https://www.cabidigitallibrary.org/doi/10.1079/cabicompendium.115969 |journal=CABI Compendium |volume=CABI Compendium |article-number=115969 |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.115969|doi-access=free }}</ref> ''O. engelmannii'' range extends from [[California]] to [[Louisiana]] in the United States, and from [[Sonora]] (state) and [[Chihuahua (state)|Chihuahua]] (state), to the [[Tamaulipan matorral]] in north and [[Tamaulipas|central Tamaulipas]].<ref name="grin"/>

Although found occasionally in the [[Mojave Desert]], it tends to be replaced by ''[[Opuntia basilaris]]'', which does not need the summer rain.

[[Naturalisation (biology)|Naturalised]] in southern and eastern [[Africa]], including [[Loisaba]] in [[Kenya]], where they are considered invasive.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mbonani |first1=Siphosenkosi |last2=Glennon |first2=Kelsey L. |last3=Byrne |first3=Marcus J. |date=2022 |title=A morphometric and genetic investigation of Opuntia engelmannii population variation in Africa |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/wre.12550 |journal=Weed Research |language=en |volume=62 |issue=5 |pages=307–317 |doi=10.1111/wre.12550 |bibcode=2022WeedR..62..307M |issn=1365-3180|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="LucidKeys" /> ''O. engelmannii'' was also reported in Spain in the early 2000s and remains invasive<ref name=":1" />.

==Description==
''O. engelmannii'' is generally shrubby, with dense clumps up to 3.5 metres (11 ft) high, usually with no apparent trunk. The pads, or cladodes, are green (rarely blue-green), obovate to round, about 15–30 cm long and 12–20 cm wide. In the [[Sonoran Desert]], terminal pads face predominantly east-west, so as to maximize the absorption of solar radiation during summer rains. The cladodes make up the stem and are the primary photosynthetic structure.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last1=Loflin |first1=Brian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Fn19h5l-4pEC |title=Texas Cacti: A Field Guide |last2=Loflin |first2=Shirley |date=2009-10-26 |publisher=Texas A&M University Press |isbn=978-1-60344-108-7 |language=en}}</ref> ''O. engelmannii'' typically grows in high altitude desert, where lower atmospheric pressure increases water stress and may make gas exchange difficult <ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Eickmeier |first=William G. |date=1979 |title=Eco-physiological Differences between High and Low Elevation CAM Species in Big Bend National Park, Texas |journal=The American Midland Naturalist |volume=101 |issue=1 |pages=118–126 |doi=10.2307/2424907 |jstor=2424907 |issn=0003-0031}}</ref>, leading to a reliance on CAM photosynthesis for more efficient gas exchange and less water lost in the process <ref name=":3" />.

The [[Glochid|glochids]] are initially yellow and brown with age. Cactus spines are nonvascularized, modified leaves that arise from areoles and are usually in clumps.<ref name=":2" /> Spines are extremely variable, with anywhere from 1-8 per areole, and are often absent from lower areoles; they are yellow to white, slightly flattened, and 1–6 cm long. Spines harden from the top down and develop a waxy cuticle.<ref name=":2" /> The spines do not photosynthesize.<ref name=":2" /> The spines primarily serve as defense. However, the spines can also facilitate asexual reproduction: by latching onto animal fur; in the process of disentangling the animal may carry off a cladode which might later dislodge and grow a new plant.<ref name=":2" />

The ''Opuntia'' genus has both tap roots and adventitious roots<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Weaver |first=John E. (John Ernest) |url=http://archive.org/details/ecologicalrelati00weav |title=The ecological relations of roots |date=1919 |publisher=Washington, Carnegie institution of Washington |others=The Library of Congress}}</ref> with some taproots acting as water storage.<ref name=":2" /> Deeper roots act as an anchor and absorb water from deeper stores.  Shallow roots spread over a large area to absorb rainfall quickly.<ref name=":4" /> ''Opuntia'' species are notable for the development of both types of roots from cladode areoles. This is especially useful for propagation, wherein separated cladodes are capable of developing roots and new shoots from the areoles,  to produce a new functional plant separate from the original.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Snyman |first=H. A. |date=2006-06-01 |title=A greenhouse study on root dynamics of cactus pears, Opuntia ficus-indica and O. robusta |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140196305002272 |journal=Journal of Arid Environments |volume=65 |issue=4 |pages=529–542 |doi=10.1016/j.jaridenv.2005.10.004 |bibcode=2006JArEn..65..529S |issn=0140-1963|url-access=subscription }}</ref> 

''Opuntia'' species tend to be colonized by arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi<ref name=":5">{{Cite thesis |url=https://opensiuc.lib.siu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?referer=&httpsredir=1&article=1089&context=uhp_theses|author=Sean Andrew Whitcomb|location=
Southern Illinois University Carbondale|degree=Honors |title=Mycorrhizal associations in Opuntia humifusa in southern Illinois|access-date=2025-12-09 |website=opensiuc.lib.siu.edu}}</ref>. Mycorrhizae colonize ''Opuntia'' plants more in the summer months than in the winter months and when there is plenty of water around.<ref name=":5" /> Mycorrhizae help to alleviate drought stress in ''Opuntia'' plants.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lahbouki |first1=Soufiane |last2=Ben-Laouane |first2=Raja |last3=Anli |first3=Mohamed |last4=Boutasknit |first4=Abderrahim |last5=Ait-Rahou |first5=Youssef |last6=Ait-El-Mokhtar |first6=Mohamed |last7=El Gabardi |first7=Soumaya |last8=Douira |first8=Allal |last9=Wahbi |first9=Said |last10=Outzourhit |first10=Abdelkader |last11=Meddich |first11=Abdelilah |date=2022-04-01 |title=Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and/or organic amendment enhance the tolerance of prickly pear (Opuntia ficus-indica) under drought stress |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S014019632100269X |journal=Journal of Arid Environments |volume=199 |article-number=104703 |doi=10.1016/j.jaridenv.2021.104703 |issn=0140-1963|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The flowers are yellow, occasionally reddish, and 6-9 cm in diameter and length.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last=Bowers |first=Janice E. |date=2004 |title=Temporal Variation in Longevity of Opuntia Engelmannii (cactaceae) Flowers |journal=Madroño |volume=51 |issue=3 |pages=280–286 |jstor=41425547 |issn=0024-9637}}</ref> The flowers are hermaphroditic with inferior ovaries.<ref name=":6" /> Their stamens are thigmotropically sensitive.<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last1=Grant |first1=Verne |last2=Hurd |first2=Paul D. |date=1979-03-01 |title=Pollination of the southwestern Opuntias |journal=Plant Systematics and Evolution |language=en |volume=133 |issue=1 |pages=15–28 |doi=10.1007/BF00985876 |bibcode=1979PSyEv.133...15G |issn=1615-6110}}</ref> Flowering is in April and May, with blooms lasting 1-2 days each. Single-day blooms open around 11AM and remain open for 6 hours. Blooms lasting 2 days tend to open around 10AM and remain open until 4:30PM on day one. On the second day they open from 8:30AM to 2:00PM. This results in an average total bloom time of 12 hours.<ref name=":6" /> Flowers produce nectar as a pollinator attractant, and ''O. engelmannii'' is noted to produce more nectar than other members of ''Opuntia''.<ref name=":6" /> 

Members of the ''Opuntia'' genus undergo cross pollination, but also tend to be self-compatible. Cross-breeding between species in the ''Opuntia'' genus has also been observed.<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last1=Reyes-Agüero |first1=J. A. |last2=Aguirre R. |first2=J. R. |last3=Valiente-Banuet |first3=A. |date=2006-03-01 |title=Reproductive biology of Opuntia: A review |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140196305001564 |journal=Journal of Arid Environments |volume=64 |issue=4 |pages=549–585 |doi=10.1016/j.jaridenv.2005.06.018 |bibcode=2006JArEn..64..549R |issn=0140-1963|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Pollinators include [[Solitary bee|solitary bees]] and [[Sap beetle|sap beetles]]. Most pollinators of ''O. engelmannii'' are polylectic (pollinate unrelated species), but several known pollinators have specialized for ''Opuntia'' <ref name=":7" />, including members of the families ''Anthophorini'' (previously known as ''Anthophoridae'' <ref>{{Cite book |last=Michener |first=Charles Duncan |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bu_1gmY13FIC |title=The Bees of the World |date=2000 |publisher=JHU Press |isbn=978-0-8018-6133-8 |language=en}}</ref>), ''Andrenidae'', and ''Megachilidae'', primarily consisting of solitary bees.<ref name=":7" /> Large and medium bees are considered the most beneficial for inter-plant pollination.<ref name=":7" /> Beetles and smaller bees typically fall into the category of "pollen thieves," as they often take pollen without effectively pollinating the plant.<ref name=":7" /> 

The purple fleshy fruits are 3.5 to 9 cm long, and 2-4 cm wide. They are spineless and glabrous, and are often ovate-elongate or barrel-shaped.<ref name=":1" /> The fruits are sweet and consumed by several animals, including humans.<ref name=":1" />

''Opuntia'' seeds are ovoid or lens shaped, averaging 0.45 cm long, 0.35 cm wide, and 0.16 cm thick. The seed funiculus is thick and white, and embryos tend to be curved.<ref name=":8" /> ''O. engelmannii'' fruits typically have an average of 144 - 172 seeds.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bowers |first=Janice E. |date=1997 |title=The Effect of Drought on Engelmann Prickly Pear (Cactaceae: Opuntia engelmannii) Fruit and Seed Production |journal=The Southwestern Naturalist |volume=42 |issue=2 |pages=240–242 |jstor=30055270 |issn=0038-4909}}</ref> The seeds can remain viable in the soil for at least 19 months prior to germination.<ref name=":1" /> In its North American range, ''O. engelmannii'' seeds are often distributed by coyotes.

== Uses ==
The fruits were a reliable summer food for [[Native Americans in the United States|Native American]] tribes.<ref>[http://herb.umd.umich.edu/herb/search.pl?searchstring=Opuntia%20engelmannii&searchlimit=100 U. of Michigan: Native American Ethnobotany Database]</ref> The [[Tohono O'odham]] of the Sonoran Desert in particular classified the fruits by color, time of ripening, and how well they kept in storage.

''O. engelmannii'' is cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]], for use in [[xeriscape|drought tolerant]] gardens, container plantings, and [[natural landscaping]] projects.<ref name="Arizona-Pima">[http://ag.arizona.edu/pima/gardening/aridplants/Opuntia_engelmannii.html Master Gardeners of the University of Arizona Pima County Cooperative Extension — ''Opuntia engelmannii'']</ref>

''O. engelmannii'' has also been used as a living hedge and cattle fodder.<ref name=":1" /> These functions, paired with a capacity to survive drought, led to its import to various locations in Africa.
